title: Is there a trustworthy numerical oracle for FDA Appendix C?
raised_by: PR #61, as the feasibility question itself
status_note: RESOLVED as a question answered, not as an obstacle removed. The investigation set out to establish whether an oracle exists and concluded that a PARTIAL one does: the estimate and the covariance parameters are checkable, the Satterthwaite denominator df is not. That is a finding about the available tooling, not a defect in anything.
what_is_established: The model, completely, including the exact FA0(2) parameterisation and the five covariance parameters named individually.
The missing-data rule, from FDA section III rather than inferred: PROC MIXED is an AVAILABLE CASE analysis that 'uses all observed data'.

Two regulator-published worked data sets with raw data, published point estimates, published 90% confidence intervals and published within-subject CVs - for THIS model, published by EMA, computed in SAS 9.1.
A partial oracle: nlme reproduces the point estimate to the published precision on both data sets and the within-subject CVs to within 0.1 percentage points.
One Satterthwaite df value, recovered indirectly and well conditioned: approximately 19.60 for Data set II.

what_is_missing.gap: an independent implementation of Satterthwaite df for THIS model
what_is_missing.why_it_blocks: df sets the width of the 90% CI and therefore the BE decision. An implementation that reproduces the estimate and the SE but not the df produces a correct point estimate inside a wrong interval, which is a wrong regulatory decision wearing the right numbers.
Without it, SE and df cannot be separated: the published CI constrains only their product t(df)*SE. nlme's SE can be checked against that product only where the recovery is well conditioned.

what_is_missing.gap: datasets covering the roles this package requires for tier 3
what_is_missing.why_it_blocks: Two data sets exist, both broadly central. PR #61 point 13 asks for balanced, unbalanced, heteroscedastic residuals, materially different subject variances, and a near-boundary decision. Synthetic cases cannot be added because generating their expected values needs the oracle that is missing.

requirements: 4. Satterthwaite denominator df for the T-R contrast
r_package_comparison.rule: A package is not an oracle unless all four hold.

nlme.how: random = list(SUBJ = pdSymm(~ TRT - 1)) gives the full 2x2 subject-level covariance, positive-definite by construction as FA0(2) is; weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | TRT) gives the treatment-specific residual variances. Five parameters, matching FDA.

lme4_lmerTest.why: lme4 estimates a single residual variance and has no varIdent equivalent. FDA's REPEATED/GRP=TRT requires one per treatment. lmerTest's Satterthwaite df is genuine and is computed on the wrong covariance structure, which makes it the most dangerous of the three: a Satterthwaite-labelled df for a model that is not Appendix C.

demonstrated_not_asserted.reading: On the UNBALANCED data set the wrong residual structure moves the point estimate by 0.136 percentage points, where nlme and glmmTMB land within 0.002. This is the limitation showing up as a number rather than as a claim about the package's features - and it is exactly the size of error a plausible-but-wrong implementation would produce.

the_sharpest_result_in_this_investigatio.what: lmerTest computes a GENUINE Satterthwaite df, and it is not SAS's.
the_sharpest_result_in_this_investigatio.consequence: t(35.94) = 1.6890 against t(19.60) = 1.7264 is a 2.2% NARROWER half-width. On a borderline study that is a different BE decision.
the_sharpest_result_in_this_investigatio.why_it_matters_most: This is the failure mode the whole investigation exists to guard against. lmerTest's Satterthwaite is correctly implemented; it is applied to a covariance structure that is not Appendix C, and the result is a df that looks principled, carries the right label, and is wrong by a factor of 1.8. An oracle cannot be accepted on the strength of the word 'Satterthwaite' - only on the strength of the model it is computed for.

glmmTMB.verdict: NOT AN ORACLE, BUT A SECOND PARTIAL ONE
glmmTMB.why: us(0 + TRT | SUBJ) and dispformula = ~ TRT express requirements 1-3. Inference is Wald: standard errors from the observed information and NORMAL quantiles, with no denominator df at all. z = 1.6449 against t(19.6) = 1.7264 is 4.7% on the half-width for Data set II, which moves a borderline decision.
glmmTMB.why_it_matters_anyway: It is an INDEPENDENT implementation of the same five-parameter structure, written in a different language against a different optimiser. Where it agrees with nlme, the agreement is evidence about the estimate and the SE that neither package could supply alone.
caveats: reported 'Model convergence problem; singular convergence (7)' on Data set II

mmrm.why: mmrm is a marginal model with no G side. Appendix C's marginal covariance is Z G Z' + R, a PATTERNED 5-parameter matrix whose pattern depends on which periods carry T and R and therefore differs by sequence. mmrm's structures are indexed by visit and would give an unpatterned 10-parameter 4x4 - a richer and different model. Assessed from the package's documented design rather than by fitting.

r_package_comparison.corroborating_observation: replicateBE, the established R package for replicate bioequivalence, implements EMA Method A and Method B and NOT Method C - despite already depending on nlme, lmerTest and pbkrtest. That the leading R package in this exact domain stops short of the FDA model is evidence about the R ecosystem rather than about anyone's effort.

estimate_and_se_conclusion.reading: Two independent implementations of the same five-parameter structure - different languages, different optimisers - reproduce EMA's published point estimate to within 0.003 percentage points on both data sets, and agree with each other on the standard error EXACTLY on the balanced data set and to 0.27% on the unbalanced one. The estimate therefore has a usable oracle; the SE has one on balanced data and a 0.27% band on unbalanced data.
estimate_and_se_conclusion.why_the_unbalanced_se_differs: NOT_DETERMINED. Candidate causes are the REML optimum being flatter with 8 incomplete subjects, and the two packages parameterising the covariance differently (pdSymm Cholesky against glmmTMB's us()). Distinguishing them would need the SAS value, which is not published.

data_set_ii.sensitivity: a 0.1% change in the SE moves the recovered df by 0.4
data_set_ii.plausible: yes - 24 subjects, 72 observations; the T-R contrast in a partial replicate is substantially between-subject, so an effective df near the subject count is expected
data_set_ii.method: t = half_width / SE from EMA's published CI and nlme's SE, inverted

data_set_i.sensitivity: a 0.1% change in the SE moves the recovered df by 773
data_set_i.plausible: NO - exceeds the 298 observations, which is impossible for this model
data_set_i.why: the implied t of 1.6477 sits 0.0028 above the normal limit 1.6449, and dt/d(df) vanishes there. The recovery is uninformative for this data set and is reported as such rather than quoted.

satterthwaite_conclusion.corroborated_by_a_second_se: nlme and glmmTMB give the SAME standard error on Data set II to five decimals (0.030317), and both therefore imply the same SAS df of 19.603. lme4 - which fits the WRONG residual structure - gives 0.030394 and implies 20.663. So the recovered df is not resting on one package's arithmetic, and the one package that disagrees is the one already known to be fitting a different model.
satterthwaite_conclusion.what_this_buys: One indirect df target, now supported by two independent SEs rather than one. A future Python implementation computing Satterthwaite df for Data set II and landing near 19.6 would be meaningful corroboration. It remains ONE number, on ONE data set, and is not a validated df.
satterthwaite_conclusion.what_it_does_not_buy: Anything for Data set I, where the recovery is ill conditioned and returns an impossible answer; and nothing at all for the unbalanced case, the heteroscedastic case, or a near-boundary decision - which is where a df method is most likely to be wrong and matters most.

missing_data_conclusion.rule: available case analysis - PROC MIXED uses all observed data
missing_data_conclusion.source: FDA, Statistical Approaches to Establishing Bioequivalence, May 2026, section III (missing data), which contrasts PROC MIXED with PROC GLM's complete case analysis
missing_data_conclusion.quoted: An available case analysis could be done using SAS PROC MIXED, which uses all observed data
missing_data_conclusion.consequence: Appendix C's inclusion rule is neither Appendix G's (which requires both reference replicates for sWR) nor EMA Method A's, and is the most permissive of the three. PR #60 established that regulator-specific inclusion rules materially change results, so this was taken from the source rather than borrowed from a neighbouring model.
missing_data_conclusion.corroboration: Data set I contains 8 subjects with missing periods and nlme, fitting all 298 observations, reproduces EMA's published Method C estimate to 0.0012 percentage points.

sas_ondemand_for_academics.why: Its licence prohibits commercial use, and work intended to support a regulatory submission is commercial. Ruled out on licence rather than on capability.

licensed_sas_environment.why: If one exists it could settle this investigation outright: one PROC MIXED run on the two published data sets would give the SE and the df directly. This is a question for the project owner, not a technical obstacle.

published_sas_output.what: EMA/618604/2008 Rev. 13 section 3.3 records that SAS 9.1 produced the Method C results. Point estimates, 90% CIs and within-subject CVs are published for two data sets whose raw data is in the same annex.
published_sas_output.what_is_absent: standard errors and denominator degrees of freedom

sas_feasibility.runtime_dependency: None proposed. be-stats must never depend on SAS, and nothing here would make it.

leading_full_oracle_candidate.name: ReplicateBE.jl
leading_full_oracle_candidate.claim: implements the FDA guidance model, described by its own documentation as EMA Method C, with FA0(2)/CSH random effects, treatment-specific residual variances and Satterthwaite df
leading_full_oracle_candidate.validation_claim_quoted: ReplicateBE is compliant to SAS/SPSS when comparing the following parameters: REML estimate, variance components estimate, fixed effect estimate, standard error of fixed effect estimate; Satterthwaite degree of freedom (DF) estimate is equal with SAS/SPSS DF estimate for full-replicated basic bioequivalence balanced and unbalanced datasets (2x2x4, 2x2x3)
leading_full_oracle_candidate.why_not: It requires a Julia toolchain in the validation container, which is a material addition and was out of scope for a feasibility PR. Its claims are recorded as claims.
leading_full_oracle_candidate.licence_note: GPL-3.0 is compatible with using it as an ORACLE - running it and comparing numbers creates no derivative work. Copying its code into be-stats would be a different question and is not proposed.

what_would_unblock_this: One PROC MIXED run on the two EMA data sets in a licensed SAS environment, reporting the SE and the Satterthwaite df. This is the shortest path and settles the question completely.
OR: adding Julia and ReplicateBE.jl to the validation container and verifying its SAS-agreement claims against the two published data sets - which would establish the estimate, SE and df together.

EITHER of those also makes the additional dataset roles reachable, because expected values could then be generated for balanced, unbalanced, heteroscedastic, unequal-subject-variance and near-boundary cases.
effect_on_existing_methods: NONE. FDA HVD below sWR = 0.294 still selects STANDARD_ABE and returns NOT DECIDED; FDA NTI criterion (b) remains unavailable. Both for the same reason, unchanged: Appendix C is not implemented.
